old: Rules with improved deduction logic
new: Base truth for speedups

old: Not the same shape. If both sides can only be the same shape (two identical polyominoes, or two small pieces that can only be a domino), it is impossible. A side left with one possible shape takes that shape away from the other side.
new: Not the same shape. If a link would make both sides of the delta the same shape (two identical polyominoes for example), it makes it impossible. This means it should be walled. This is also true if we know what shape a side would be without knowing its position (an area number 2 is always a domino, no matter where it goes).

old: Must grow. If one side is already a finished piece and the other side matches its shape right now, the other side can not stop there: it has to grow.
new: Must grow. If one side of the delta is decided and the other side matches it currently, we know it must grow at least one more tile.

old: Same size. A 4 on one side makes the other side a 4, and so on down a line of Gemini walls. Two same-size pieces sharing an area of 9 tiles are 4 tiles or fewer each.
new: Same size. If a side is known to be size 4, then the other side is size 4 as well. This check is also used to know what the maximum size for a shape next to a gemini can be, if the total area is 8 then that shape will be size 4 at best.

old: Same shape. A polyomino on one side gives its shape to the other side. If the shape on one side contains a 1x4, the other side needs one too.
new: Same shape. A polyomino on one side gives its shape to the other side. This also applies if the shape isn't finished : a shape on one side contains a 1x4? the other side needs one too.

old: Lines anchor the copy. When both sides have a closed straight line of the same length and one side can not make a second one, the copy must send line onto line: only 4 ways are left (two directions, two mirrors). The solver copies the known tiles and walls across each way, and the ways that break are dropped.
new: Same shape advanced. When a side is known to contain a unique shape (for example it has a 2x3 and it won't be able to make another one), if the other side also contains that shape we know it is exactly that instance. We can then test rotations/symmetry using this point as the common point, which is fast to test as there are at most 8.

old: Room for the whole chain. Pieces on a chain all have different sizes, so they need at least 1 + 2 + 3 + ... tiles: a closed area of 5 tiles can not hold a chain of 3 walls. Three touching pieces that can each only be 1 or 2 tiles can not all differ.
new: Room for whole chains. When a chain of inequality exists, we know the area it will take will be at least n(n+1)/2 (1+2+3...+n). If the area needed to hold it is too small it would break, so we can't place wall in places that would force a chain to be too restrained.

old: Size across the wall. A known 2 next to a Difference 2 makes the other side exactly 4 (0 is not a size). A tile closed in by walls is a known 1.
new: Size across the wall. Since size needs to be strictly positive, a known 2 next to a difference 2 makes the other side size 4. We don't even need for exact size to use this idea, if a shape is known to be between size 2 and 4 and it hits a difference 5, the other side must be between size 7 and 9.

old: Odd and even. An odd N makes one side odd and the other even; an even N makes both sides odd or both even. Three pieces that all touch through odd Differences are impossible.
new: Odd and even. An odd difference makes one side odd and the other even and an even difference makes both sides odd or both sides even. We can use this idea to eliminate links that would create parity issue without having to check for all possible sizes.

old: Two numbers, two pieces. The pieces across a Difference 2 and a Difference 3 of the same piece can never have the same size, so they are different pieces.
new: Two numbers, two pieces. If a piece touches two difference walls with one being 2 and the other being 4, the other side of those walls can never connect, no matter what the original piece does.

old: The numbers must fit. Every number needs a whole piece of its size: a 6 and a 4 do not fit on 9 tiles. Two touching 3s with room for only one piece of 3 are linked; if each needs its own piece, there is a wall.
new: The numbers must fit. Adding numbers up should always be lower than the total area. if a wall would make that area too small it is a link. For example a 6 and a 4 can't be inside a size 8. This is also used to know that two area numbers with the same number must connect if their sum is bigger than the total area (two 5 must be together in an area 9).

old: No tile left over. When the numbers of an area sum up to its size, every tile must end up in a numbered piece, so a group with no number has to grow to one it can still reach.
new: No tile left over. In a similar idea, if the sum of all the numbers is EXACTLY equal to the area (with no way to merge two number together), then every tile must link to an area number. this is especially useful for far away tiles, since we now know they must connect to one of the area numbers.

old: Counting. Every type appears once per piece, so uneven counts are impossible. Two roses of the same type are never one piece: neighbouring ones get a wall.
new: Counting. Since every type appears once per piece, two pieces with a rose in common are walled off instantly. Uneven counts are impossible so a wall that would force uneven count is a link. This also makes puzzle with global uneven count get rejected instantly.

old: Narrow passages. If a narrow passage splits the roses into uneven counts, the extra roses on one side must join the extra roses on the other side through it. An area closed off with one rose of each type is a single piece.
new: Counting Advanced. The extension of the uneven counting, narrow passages must be passed through if they would leave uneven count, this also works for slightly bigger passages if the difference of rose amount is bigger to the same degree. A 2 wide passage with three red one blue on the left and three blue one red on the right must have the passage linked to allow the connection for 2 shapes.

old: Who goes with whom. Like the ends of a Flow puzzle, the solver lists every way to group the roses into pieces. Two roses that are never grouped are different pieces.
new: Who goes with whom. Similarly to a Flow puzzle, the solver lists every way to group the remaining roses into pieces. Pretty useful when puzzle has a lot of different roses in small packs.

old: Must fit the shape. The piece has the polyomino's size, and the tiles already together must fit in the shape: with a shape that has no line of 3, two tiles in a row get a wall at both ends.
new: Must fit the shape. The piece has the polyomino's size, it is also considered like an area number. Also tiles already together must fit in the shape. So if a shape has no line of length 3, two tiles in a row instantly get a wall at both ends.

old: Where the polyomino can go. The solver tests each place the shape can go over the polyomino: tiles every place covers are linked, edges on the border of every place are walls. Two identical polyominoes too far apart for one place are different pieces.
new: Where the polyomino can go. The solver tests each place the shape can go over the polyomino, if in every universe two shapes must be linked they are linked (same with walls). This helps identify that two identical polyominoes where the merge causes all possible tiling to fail must be different pieces.

old: 1 and 4. A 1 links all the tiles round the corner, a 4 walls them all.
new: 1 and 4. A 1 links all the tiles round the corner, a 4 walls them all. Pretty trivial :)

old: 2 and 3. A 2 is exactly two walls. A 3 is three walls, or four if one piece wraps round the corner; when no piece can wrap (too small, or no way round), a 3 with three walls known links the fourth.
new: 2 and 3. A 2 is exactly two walls, either in a bend or a straight line. So if two walls or two links are decided we know the other two states. A 3 is more tricky, as it can be three walls, or four if one piece wraps around the corner. When no piece can wrap (too small, or no way round), a 3 with three walls known links the fourth.

old: Outline and inward corners. Only two tiles touch an outline corner: a 1 links them, a 2 walls them, a 3 or 4 is impossible. Three tiles touch an inward corner (next to a hole or a notch in the board): a 3 there is three walls.
new: Edges of puzzle. A 1 or a 2 at the edge of the puzzle is respectively a link or a wall. Similarly a 1 or a 3 at an inward corner is two links or two walls. And more is impossible. (this is also true for walls the solver discovers midway)

old: Count the sides. Once enough sides are known the rest follow: a 1 with its wall found links the other three, a 1 on the outline links its three inner sides.
new: Count the sides. If a palisade has already enough links or walls known, the solver can instantly input the rest. With a straight 2 palisade with a wall already known bottom of it, the solver puts the wall on the opposite side, and two links on the left and right directly.

old: Palisades together. Palisades side by side or corner to corner are solved together: a 0 next to a 3 makes their shared side the 3's only opening, so its other three sides are walls.
new: Palisades together. Palisade can have some interesting interaction when next to each other, or when diagonally adjacent. Most famous example of that is the 1 palisade and 2 palisade diagonally adjacent forces the 1 to have two links outwards. There are other cases specially with solitude that the solver can use.

old: Only two pieces. When only two pieces can exist, a straight 2 puts the tiles on its two walled sides in the same piece, and a bent 2 puts the tiles on its opposite sides in different pieces.
new: Only two pieces. When a puzzle is known to have EXACTLY two shapes in total, palisades become a very good tool to find coloring reasoning. For example no matter the orientation, the opposite side of a straight line palisade will always be the same piece/color.

old: A count is a limit. With 2 east, nothing three columns or more to the east can join, and a 0 closes its side. A detour round a wall costs tiles too, so a tile the piece can not afford to reach gets a wall.
new: A count is a limit. With a 2 east compass, nothing three columns or more to the east can join the compass. This also walls off 0 compasses instantly. If walls force a detour, it can also reduce the "reachable" even more.

old: The only way. If the piece can only get enough tiles on a side through one tile, that tile joins. Tiles in every piece that fits all the numbers are linked, tiles in none are walled off.
new: The only way. If a compass needs a lot of tiles and one of them is a choke point that leads to the count being possible, it must be linked. This is very important to know when a compass has to "wrap around". Similarly to polyomino, if in every possible compass shape two tiles are linked/walled, we can add that. (this is mostly useful for compass with all 4 direction inputted)

old: Size. Four numbers cap the piece at 1 + N + E + S + W tiles, and the numbers also give a smallest size: one number k needs k + 1 tiles.
new: Size. Size of compasses are ranges, but we can find some easy truths : A compass with four numbers cap the piece at 1 + N + E + S + W tiles. And any compass also gives a smallest size at "biggest number + 1" (the compass tile itself).

old: Two compasses. An upper compass with 3 north and a lower one with 1 north can not be one piece: everything north of the upper one is also north of the lower one. Two compasses that would need more tiles apart than the board has on one side are one piece.
new: Count doesn't match. A compass with north 3 cannot merge with another compass above it if they also have north 3. This logic is also true with the first compass being north 2, or the second compass being further away. In the opposite manner, if a tile needs to be part of two compasses, mostly from size being too big, then the two compasses must be together in the same shape.

old: Grow and stop. A group under the size with one way out takes it, and a group at the size is walled all round: on a 1x9 strip with Precision 3 both walls are found at once.
new: Grow and stop. If a shape hasn't satisfied the precision yet, and has only one way out, then it must grow out that way. Similarly if it has already satisfied the precision then it's walled off.

old: One connection. Where part of the board hangs on a single edge, counting decides it: 24 tiles behind one edge with Precision 5 need a piece to cross it, so the edge is a link. This works for every size rule.
new: The board must divide advanced. Knowing that the board must divide everything equally, when a choke point exists we can count to know how many tiles need to be poking out/in. A pocket of size 23 with precision 5 needs to be poking out through its only choke point 2 tiles.

old: Sizes that fit. 7 tiles with Minimum 3 can only use pieces of 3, 4 or 7: a 5 or a 6 would leave 2 or 1 tiles.
new: Sizes that fit. An area of size 7 with Minimum 3 can only use pieces of size 3, 4 or 7: a 5 or a 6 would leave 2 or 1 tiles and fail the minimum.

old: Too small. A group under the Minimum with one way out takes it, and one that can not reach enough tiles is impossible. A closed area under twice the Minimum is one piece.
new: Too small. Similarly to precision, if a shape has only one way out and hasn't satisfied the minimum, it has to grow that way. This also makes us know a closed area with the size strictly under twice the minimum is one piece, two pieces wouldn't fit.

old: Together with the other bound. A Minimum and a Maximum make a range: 13 tiles with pieces of 4 to 6 can only use 4s and 5s, and a 2x3 board with pieces of 3 to 5 is two pieces of 3.
new: Together with the other bound. A Minimum and a Maximum make a range: Knowing that can help reduce possible size combinations even more, sometimes it can even rule out a size completely. min 4 max 6 in a pocket of 12 can only be 4+4+4 or 6+6.

old: Too big together. Two groups that would be too big together get a wall. A closed area needs at least (tiles / Maximum) pieces: 10 tiles with Maximum 5 and only two groups make each group its own piece.
new: Too big together. When adding up two shapes size make a number above the maximum, then those two shapes must be distinct. And in puzzles where the total amount of shape is known or limited (mismatch for example) maximum allows the solver to enumerate all possible shapes and plan accordingly.

old: Together with the other bound. A Minimum and a Maximum make a range: 13 tiles with pieces of 4 to 6 can only use 4s and 5s, and a 2x3 board with pieces of 3 to 5 is two pieces of 3.
new: Together with the other bound. A Minimum and a Maximum make a range: Knowing that can help reduce possible size combinations even more, sometimes it can even rule out a size completely. min 4 max 6 in a pocket of 12 can only be 4+4+4 or 6+6.

old: Sizes. Only the bank's sizes count: straight trominoes on 7 tiles is impossible, and a domino and a pentomino on 9 tiles is only 2 + 2 + 5. The same holds for every closed area.
new: Sizes. Since every piece is a shape in the shape bank, they must all have one of their size. If the bank only holds shape of size 2 and 5, a closed area of size 9 forces the 2+2+5 combination.

old: Where a shape can go. The solver lists every placement that holds each group, and what they share is decided: straight trominoes on a 1x6 strip find the wall after the third tile.
new: Where a shape can go. With shape bank every possibility is very restrictive, so testing all possible placement is a good strategy specially with small shape banks.

old: What every shape has. If every bank shape contains a 2x2 block, so does every piece: a tile with no room for a 2x2 around it is impossible. The same goes for a bend.
new: What is in common. If every bank shape contains a 2x2 block, so does every piece. This means a straight corridor must go out in a way that allows it to contain that 2x2. This is also true if every shape doesn't contain a 2x2, but it is taken care of by the point above.

old: Enough shapes. There is 1 domino, 2 trominoes, 5 tetrominoes... A board that can not be covered with different shapes is impossible, and sizes that can not be used are dropped.
new: Enough shapes. Mismatch is a piece amount limitation, since there is 1 domino, 2 trominoes, 5 tetrominoes... so with a size limitation we can easily tell what pieces HAVE to be used, in particular a puzzle which area is equal to the total size of all shapes must have room for every, single, one.

old: A shape is used once. Once a piece is the domino, no other piece can be. Two pieces that can only be the two trominoes take both, even before knowing which is which. Two touching area numbers 2 are one piece (there is a single domino).
new: A shape is used once. Since every shape is unique, if they are already drawn, every piece that looks like it must grow to avoid breaking mismatch.

old: Room for the neighbour. A place is dropped if it leaves a neighbour room only for the same shape: a 1x4 gap can not be filled with 1x2s.
new: Room for the neighbour. If an area can be filled with a shape that would leave the remaining hole of that same shape, then it can't happen, as both would be matching and break mismatch.

old: Sizes used up. Once both trominoes are used no other piece has 3 tiles, and Inequality and Difference walls carry that further.
new: A shape is used once advanced. The solver doesn't need to check if the shape is fully drawn to know if that shape is still available in the rest of the puzzle. If two places need to be of area 3, since there exist only 2 trominoes, the rest of the puzzle can't be either of those and no size 3 can happen.

old: One size. The size divides the board and every area closed by walls: 12 tiles allow 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or 12. With one size left, groups grow to it and stop, and a tile that is the only way into a part of the board takes exactly what is left after whole pieces.
new: One size. If the puzzle is one shape, then the puzzle has one size. This means the shape can only be one size that divides the total area of the puzzle. If the puzzle is of size 12, then the shape can't be of size 5.

old: One shape for every group. Every group known to be one piece must fit in the shape: a bent group of 3 and a straight group of 3 rule out size 3. With one shape left, every group needs a place for it, like a polyomino.
new: One shape for every group. Every part of the puzzle that is known can act as small pocket of knowledge about the shape as a whole. If we know the shape contains a 1x3 and the 2x2 then it must be of size 5 or more.

old: Every tile needs the shape. Every tile of the board must be covered by some placement of the shape: a size where no shape can reach every tile (a dead end at the end of a 1-wide arm, a 2x2 pocket) is dropped.
new: One shape for every group advanced. This idea of pocket of knowledge can be pushed further, if we know from a compass that the shape must fit inside a 5x5 square as a whole, then finding the correct shape can get a lot easier as any shape that breaks that size limit are instantly dismissed without testing the tiling. Combining known sub-shapes that must fit inside the true shape and size limitation from puzzle grid or clue we can go through all possibilities very quickly.

old: Neighbours lose a shape. A piece known to be a shape takes it from every piece across a wall: with a bank of a domino and two trominoes, the piece next to a domino has 3 tiles. Two touching pieces known to be the same shape are one piece.
new: Neighbours lose a shape. When a piece is already decided, every neighbor that looks like it must grow, this is especially useful with small shapes like the 1x1, or with shape bank.

old: Two shapes. With only two possible shapes, neighbours alternate like a chessboard: an odd loop of walls is impossible, and no corner has exactly three walls.
new: Two shapes. And when only two possible shapes are used in the puzzle, we know the solution must always alternate, like a checkerboard pattern. This also makes us know a corner can't have exactly 3 walls.

old: Neighbours lose a size. With sizes 2 to 4, the piece next to a 2 has at least 3 tiles. Two touching area numbers 2 are one piece.
new: Neighbours lose a size. Exactly the same idea that mingle shape had, but even more restrictive, if a shape is decided neighbouring shapes of the same size must grow.

old: Two sizes. With only two possible sizes, neighbours alternate like a chessboard: an odd loop of walls is impossible, and no corner has exactly three walls.
new: Two sizes. And exactly like mingle shape, with only 2 sizes the solution is also a sort of checkerboard pattern, so all corners of exactly 3 walls are banned.

old: One symbol each. N symbols make N pieces, and two symbols never share one: neighbouring symbols get a wall.
new: One symbol each. Since N symbols make N pieces, this rule allows us to know the total amount of pieces. Also two neighbouring pieces that each already hold a symbol can't merge and are walled off.

old: Reaching a symbol. A group with no symbol must grow to one, so a wall that would cut it off from all of them is a link. A closed area with one symbol is one piece.
new: Reaching a symbol. A group with no symbol must grow to one, so a wall that would cut it off from all of them is a link and a closed area with one symbol needs to be one piece.

old: Fill the box. Tiles of one piece fill the box round them: two tiles at opposite corners of a 2x3 link all six.
new: Fill the box. Tiles known to be one piece need to fill everything in the middle to be a rectangle, so an L tetromino needs to be a 2x3. The solver doesn't need to know the tiles are already linked for that, knowing they will eventually be part of the same shape is enough to fill the whole middle.

old: Walls run straight. A wall can not stop in the open or turn a corner: at each inner corner it runs straight, makes a T or a cross.
new: Walls run straight. At every corner, there can never be exactly 2 walls that form a bend, otherwise the other two links would create a bend tromino. This means every corner either runs straight, has 3 walls, or has 4 walls. (or 0)

old: Where the rectangle can go. For a piece of known size the solver lists every rectangle that fits, and what they share is decided. A group already shut on one side (wall, hole, board edge) can not grow past it.
new: What placement fits the size. When a piece's size is known, it's very fast to check every placement of it with boxy as the amount of possible rectangles is very small. This is done to know what link is always there and what wall is always there.

old: Prime sizes. However the size is known (an area number, Difference or Inequality walls, ...), a prime size is a strip: a piece of 7 is a 1x7, and where 7 tiles do not fit across, it runs up and down.
new: Prime sizes. To go further, when the size of a piece is known and is a prime number then the shape is a strip: a size of 7 is always a 1x7, and finding way to fit it into the puzzle often leads to knowing if it is horizontal or vertical.

old: At least 3 tiles. A single tile and a domino are rectangles, so every piece has 3 tiles or more.
new: At least 3 tiles. Title says it all ! The 1x1 and 1x2 are both rectangles, so non boxy is also minimum 3 so minimum logic also applies.

old: Keep growing. A group that is a rectangle so far is not finished: with one way out, that edge is a link. A closed strip or a small closed box is impossible.
new: Keep growing. If a shape is currently a rectangle, it has to grow no matter what. And if it only has one way to grow then that needs to be a link.

old: Three walls. Three walls at a corner make the fourth a link.
new: Three walls. If we know three walls at a corner, we know the 4th is a link, pretty self explanatory.

old: Poking-in corners. Where two walls meet at a right angle pointing into the board (next to a hole), the tile diagonal to it must join one of its two neighbours: it can never be a one-tile piece. Two pieces (or holes) touching only at a corner are impossible.
new: Poking-in corners. Where two walls meet at a right angle pointing into the board (or from a hole), the tile diagonal to it has to join one of its two neighbours. If it didn't, it would instantly create 4 walls. Two pieces (or holes) with touching corners are impossible. This helps reduce possible placement for polyomino and such.

old: 'a clue in it is not valid'
new: `a clue in the puzzle isn't valid`
